Which Risks Face Commonwealth Bank (ASX:CBA) After the Rate Rise?
sum: - The nation's largest lender enters a tighter rate setting with its own economists downgrading the growth picture.
- Dearer money can support lending margins while squeezing borrowers and slowing credit demand.
- A rival's jump in bad debts has sharpened attention on asset quality across the sector.

Commonwealth Bank (ASX:CBA) Financial Services Commonwealth Bank of Australia (ASX:CBA) 167.51 AUD +1.220 0.734% Last Updated at: 2026-11-06T05:10:00Z is confronting a harder lending backdrop this week after the Reserve Bank lifted the cash rate again and the bank's own economists slashed their growth outlook, leaving credit demand and loan quality as the main questions hanging over Australia's biggest lender. As Commonwealth Bank continues operating within the ASX 20, growing attention is also being directed towards ASX Financial Stocks as companies across the sector navigate changing market conditions.
For readers watching the CBA share price ASX trend today, margins and capital remain central.

The central bank's Tuesday decision was its latest increase of a bruising year and took the cash rate to its highest level since the global financial crisis. The vote was divided, which matters: a split board tells lenders that the next move is far from settled.

The major banks responded quickly by passing the increase on to variable mortgage customers, with new rates starting next week. For Commonwealth Bank, which has among the country's largest home loan books, that repricing reaches a very large group of borrowers at once.

NAB shares slump 7% to three-week low as FY26 cash earnings miss
sum: Investing.com -- National Australia Bank shares slumped on Thursday after the lender reported weaker full-year earnings, with higher credit impairment charges and software-related costs weighing on profitability.
Shares fell 7.5% to A$38.08, touching their lowest level since October 12 and sharply underperforming the broader S&P/ASX 200, which was up 1.8% in morning trading.

Cash earnings fell 13.4% to A$6.14 billion for the year ended September 30, missing the Visible Alpha consensus estimate of about A$6.33 billion. Statutory net profit attributable declined 9.1% to A$6.14 billion, below analysts' A$6.45 billion estimate.

Net operating income increased 5.8% to A$22.01 billion, supported by higher lending volumes and improved margins. However, credit impairment charges jumped 85.7% to A$1.55 billion from A$833 million a year earlier, including a A$403 million increase in collective provisions reflecting a more challenging economic outlook.

The bank's cash earnings included A$1.35 billion in large notable items, primarily related to a change in its software capitalisation policy. Excluding these items, cash earnings remained broadly flat at A$7.09 billion, also below analysts' A$7.24 billion estimate on an adjusted basis.
NAB's net interest margin (NIM) improved 6 basis points to 1.80%, as at quarter end.
The increase in credit charges included A$1.08 billion in individually assessed provisions, primarily related to business lending customers.

Why bonds are back on investors’ radars
sum: Australian investors have long looked to dividend-paying shares for income, but higher interest rates are changing the alternatives available to them.
After more than a decade in which low rates reduced the returns available from many fixed income investments, bond yields have risen in 2026, lifting the income available.

The shift has brought an asset class often overlooked by self-directed investors back into focus, Senior Vice President, Global Wealth Management with global bond investment firm PIMCO Kanish Chugh said in a CommSec Executive Series interview.
Chugh said Australian investors had traditionally been comfortable with shares, helped by the income available from dividends and franking credits.
But a long period of unusually low interest rates had also played a role.

“When you think about low interest rate environments that we had for much of the 2010s and early 2020s, we had this environment where Australian investors weren’t getting a high rate of return should they put their cash towards a term deposit, for example,” he said.
Chugh said the bond yields being seen in late 2026 were high compared with much of the period since the Global Financial Crisis, but less unusual when viewed over a longer timeframe.

ASX 200 Rises 0.3% as RBA Hikes Rates to 18-Year High in Split Vote, With Dovish Signals Lifting Shares Late
sum: SYDNEY — Australian shares closed higher on Tuesday after the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, as investors focused on signs the central bank may be nearing the end of its tightening campaign.
The S&P/ASX 200 index rose 30.3 points, or 0.34%, to close at 8,886.8 on Melbourne Cup day, recovering part of Monday's 0.6% decline.
The market opened strongly, with the benchmark up 0.43% to 8,894 in the first half hour of trading as gains in mining and industrial stocks lifted the index.
Gains faded around midday, and the index slipped into slightly negative territory, trading at 8,855 at 1:30 p.m. local time amid reports of fresh U.S. strikes on Iran, according to Capital Brief.
The index dipped again briefly when the RBA announced its decision at 2:30 p.m., falling about 0.15% at its session low, before rebounding sharply into the close.

The RBA raised its cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85%, its fifth increase in 2026 and the highest level since late 2008. The central bank also raised rates in February, March, May and September.
The decision was widely expected. Money markets had priced in about an 80% chance of a hike.

Wall Street rally fades as tech and AI stocks slip again
sum: A morning rally for US stocks petered out on Monday as the tech and AI industries remained shaky following their sell-off last week.
The S&P 500 sank 0.5% after erasing a gain that had reached 1.1% early in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 213 points, or 0.4%, while the Nasdaq composite fell 1.1%.

The mixed performance for indexes came even though the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 climbed. They benefited from a 7.6% drop in the price of a barrel of Brent crude to $US104.77. It's the latest yo-yo move for oil prices amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal.

The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $US70 and $US120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began, and it's been quick to reverse direction.

So have stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry, which have been shaky for months amid criticism that they surged too high and are in a bubble. Worries are growing that all the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech companies are pouring into AI data centres won't yield enough productivity and profit to make the investments worth it.

The latest profit reports from Alphabet and other Big Tech companies also showed how AI may be dragging on their own businesses. Not only did Google's parent company burn through more cash during the latest quarter, as measured by something called free cash flow, it also reported slower-than-expected growth in its search business, which raised worries about AI undercutting its cash cow. That caused Alphabet's stock to drop more than 12% on Thursday for its worst day on record.

On Monday, Alphabet initially rallied 2.6%, but it later erased the gain and then finished with a loss of 0.3%. Nvidia, meanwhile, went from an early gain of 2.6% to a drop of 1.3% following its 4.2% slide on Friday. Such swings dragged the rest of the market with them.

I'd buy these ASX dividend shares over CBA shares for income
sum: Commonwealth Bank of Australia (ASX: CBA) shares are not one of my top picks for dividend income. There are quite a few other ASX dividend shares that are more appealing for passive income.

CBA is a great bank in the Australian financial sector, though it faces a lot of competition from the likes of ANZ Group Holdings Ltd (ASX: ANZ), Westpac Banking Corp (ASX: WBC), National Australia Bank Ltd (ASX: NAB), and Macquarie Group Ltd (ASX: MQG), keeping a lid on lending margins.
In the current economic climate, I don't think CBA is likely to deliver a big dividend yield or a lot of growth.

According to the (independent) projection on CommSec, CBA is forecast to grow its annual dividend per share by just 2% to $5.15. At the time of writing, that translates into a grossed-up dividend yield of 4.4%, including franking credits.
I'm going to highlight two ASX dividend shares that could provide a better dividend yield than CBA shares and grow the dividend faster.

The first business I want to highlight is a listed investment company (LIC). LICs are very useful for passive income because they represent a portfolio of diversified assets and can turn investment profits into dividend payments.

WCM invests by targeting quality businesses with an improving economic moat. Having competitive advantages is positive to stay ahead of competitors, so having an improving economic moat is a strong sign of improving financials.

items.t: Commonwealth Bank stock: Morgan Stanley cuts target to AUD 125.00
sum: Commonwealth Bank of Australia (AU000000CBA7) faces a lower AUD 125.00 price target from Morgan Stanley, leaving the target AUD 32.17 below the ASX price of AUD 157.17, or 20.47 percent. MarketScreener reported the Morgan Stanley adjustment on October 18, 2026. Commonwealth Bank was trading at EUR 98.14 at Lang & Schwarz on October 22, 2026 at 5:12 p.m. CEST.

The analyst view sets a clear valuation reference for the bank. Morgan Stanley's AUD 125.00 target is 20.47 percent below the AUD 157.17 ASX price, a gap that places the research view well below the latest Australian quotation.

Commonwealth Bank's valuation is also higher than the comparison group. Simply Wall St lists a P/E of 24.10 for CBA against a peer average of 16.60, while Westpac is at 17.30 and National Australia Bank at 20.10. The comparison shows that the premium is not limited to one valuation measure.

The latest market capitalization is AUD 262.76 billion, with a 52-week range of AUD 146.98 to AUD 185.59. The ASX quotation stood at AUD 157.17 on October 22, 2026 at 4:12 p.m. AEDT, placing the share AUD 10.19 above its yearly low and AUD 28.42 below its yearly high.

Commonwealth Bank held its 2026 annual meeting on October 14, 2026. The investor center identifies the bank's 2026 full-year results and annual report among its reporting materials, while its business covers retail, commercial and institutional banking in Australia and New Zealand.

The contrast between AUD 157.17 in the market and AUD 125.00 in Morgan Stanley's target is the central valuation signal. A P/E of 24.18 also exceeds the 16.60 peer average, so the share price leaves less room for disappointment than the comparison banks.

The euro quotation gives German investors a separate trading view of Commonwealth Bank. The stock was trading at EUR 98.14 at Lang & Schwarz on October 22, 2026 at 5:12 p.m. CEST. The further course of trading is shown by the continuously updated real-time quote of CBA stock.

CBA stock: Morgan Stanley keeps Sell rating for Commonwealth Bank stock at AUD 125.00
sum: Commonwealth Bank of Australia (AU000000CBA7) is facing a fresh valuation test after Markets Insider reported on October 19, 2026 that Morgan Stanley maintained its Sell rating and set an AUD 125.00 price target. The euro quote was EUR 98.17 at Lang & Schwarz on October 21, 2026 at 3:31 p.m. CEST.

Commonwealth Bank reported that cash net profit after tax increased 7 percent to AUD 11.00 billion in fiscal year 2026. The bank also lifted cash earnings per share by AUD 0.44 and declared a fully franked final dividend of AUD 2.70, taking the full-year dividend to AUD 5.05 per share, according to Commonwealth Bank on October 14, 2026.

The ASX quote was AUD 157.01 at 4:19 p.m. AEDT on October 21, 2026, up 0.91 percent from the prior close of AUD 155.60. The 52-week range was AUD 146.98 to AUD 185.59, while market capitalization stood at AUD 262.5 billion.

At a price-to-earnings ratio of 24.16, CBA remained above the valuation multiples of two large Australian banking peers. ANZ Group Holdings traded at a P/E of 20.01 with a market capitalization of AUD 118.2 billion, while National Australia Bank traded at 20.80 times earnings with a market value of AUD 124.2 billion on October 21, 2026.

Morgan Stanley's AUD 125.00 target is AUD 32.01 below the ASX quote of AUD 157.01. Its Sell view therefore places more weight on valuation than on the 7 percent fiscal 2026 profit increase. The bank's own October 14 address also said growth was slowing and inflation remained elevated, while it entered fiscal year 2027 from a position of strength.

Banks weigh down ASX after US earnings spook markets
sum: Australian shares have dipped following a sharp sell-off in the major banks, after disappointing earnings from their US counterparts highlighted the challenging backdrop for financial institutions.
The S&P/ASX200 fell 56 points on Wednesday, down 0.64 per cent, to 8727.9, as the broader All Ordinaries dropped 52.5 points, or 0.59 per cent, to 8869.

The heavyweight financials sector tumbled 1.6 per cent as the big four banks sold off, after US bank earnings failed to impress investors and a shareholder address from CommBank boss Matt Comyn noted a host of local and international economic headwinds. Commonwealth Bank slumped 2.2 per cent, National Australia Bank shed 1.8 per cent, Westpac fell 1.3 per cent and ANZ Bank slid0.2 per cent.

Underwhelming US bank profits had confirmed investor fears the big institutions were leaning into their equity books, while commercial lending, deal-making (for investment banks) and fixed income had been underperforming, Capital.com analyst Kyle Rodda said.
“They just haven’t really been as profitable, and they don’t look like they’ll be as profitable going forward,” he told AAP.
“While the composition of our banks is very different, if you see a lead like that from Wall Street, you basically see a sector-wide fall.”

Miners also sold off, with gold prices still under pressure from elevated bond yields and as iron ore futures continued to linger at two-year lows. Spot gold eased slightly to $US4158 ($5938) an ounce, dragging the sub-index almost two per cent into the red.

Tech stocks slip as Wall Street hovers near its record high
sum: The S&P 500 slipped 0.1 per cent after wavering between small gains and losses. The benchmark index set a record high last Tuesday and is up 14 per cent so far this year.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.4 per cent.

Shares in roughly 64 per cent of the companies in the S&P 500 rose, led by communication services stocks. Meta Platforms rose 3.4 per cent, T-Mobile added 2.2 per cent, AT&T gained 1.4 per cent and Verizon Communications rose 2.7 per cent.
Energy stocks had some of the biggest gains as oil prices kept rising. Chevron rose 1.4 per cent.
Despite those gains, a slide in big technology stocks dragged the market into the red.

Micron Technology fell 3.9 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 2.3 per cent, Broadcom slid 1.9 per cent and Nvidia gave up 1.3 per cent. They are among several companies in the sector with big stock values that tend to have a heavy influence on the market. They have also been the driving force behind the broader market's record gains throughout the year.

Those companies could face more scrutiny from investors during this round of corporate earnings as Wall Street tries to get a better sense of whether the stock gains made during the frenzy over artificial intelligence can translate into future growth.
